test_title: PYST 38: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 14 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: When we pour acetone (nail polish remover) on our palm, we feel cold because:

options.text: it blocks nerve signals on the skin
it evaporates rapidly, absorbing heat from the palm
it reacts with water present on the palm

solution:
The correct answer is __**it evaporates rapidly, absorbing heat from the palm**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Evaporation** is a **surface phenomenon** where molecules in the liquid state gain enough energy to enter the gaseous state. This process inherently causes a **cooling effect** because the escaping high-energy molecules take thermal energy away from the surface.
 
• **Acetone**, commonly known as **nail polish remover**, is a highly **volatile liquid**. Volatile substances are those that have a high **vapor pressure** and a **low boiling point**, meaning they transition from liquid to vapor very easily at **room temperature**.
 
• When **acetone** is poured onto the palm, the molecules use the **latent heat of vaporization** required for the phase change. They absorb this necessary **thermal energy** directly from the **skin of the palm**. ***Hence, the statement that it evaporates rapidly, absorbing heat from the palm is correct.***
 
• As the **palm loses heat** to the acetone, the **temperature** of the skin surface drops. This physical change is detected by **thermoreceptors** (nerve endings) in the skin, which send signals to the brain, resulting in the sensation of **coldness**.
 
• Regarding the other options: **Statement 1** is incorrect as the cold sensation is due to heat loss from the hand, not the "release" of cold vapors. **Statement 2** is incorrect because acetone does not act as an **anesthetic** to block nerve signals in this context. **Statement 4** is incorrect because the effect is a **physical phase change**, not a **chemical reaction** with water.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Latent Heat of Vaporization**: This is the amount of **heat energy** required to change **1 kg** of a liquid into a gas at its boiling point without any change in temperature. For acetone, this value is approximately **518 kJ/kg** at its boiling point.
 
• **Boiling Point of Acetone**: Acetone has a relatively low boiling point of about **56.05°C** (**329.2 K**) compared to water, which boils at **100°C**. This low boiling point is why it feels much colder than water when placed on the skin, as it **evaporates** much faster.
 
• **Intermolecular Forces**: The reason acetone is volatile is due to its **weak intermolecular forces**. While it has **dipole-dipole interactions**, it lacks the strong **hydrogen bonding** present in water, making it easier for acetone molecules to break away from the liquid surface.
 
• **Comparison with Alcohol**: Similar to acetone, **isopropyl alcohol** (rubbing alcohol) and **ethanol** also produce a cooling sensation. These are also volatile liquids frequently used in **sanitizers** and medical swabs.
 
• **Factors Affecting Evaporation**: The rate at which a liquid like acetone evaporates depends on the **surface area** (spreading it on the palm increases the rate), **temperature**, and **humidity**. Higher temperatures and lower humidity levels **accelerate** the evaporation process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chemical Formula**: Acetone is the simplest **ketone** with the chemical formula **(CH3)2CO**. It is a colorless, flammable liquid.
 
• **Industrial Uses**: Beyond **nail polish remover**, acetone is used as a **solvent** for plastics, synthetic fibers, and in the manufacture of **methyl methacrylate**.
 
• **Biological Context**: Small amounts of acetone are produced in the **human body** through **metabolic processes** (ketosis). Excessive levels can be found in the breath of individuals with **diabetes mellitus**.
 
• **Safety**: While it provides a cooling sensation, prolonged skin contact with acetone can cause **defatting** of the skin, leading to **irritation** or **dermatitis**, as it dissolves the natural oils present on the skin surface.
